title: Non-string form field names raise AttributeError when files are attached

comments_snapshot.body: Hi, I'd like to work on this. I'll submit a PR shortly.
I’m stepping back after reading the repository’s AI policy, so this issue is available for another contributor.

Reproduced on 2.34.2 (current master), and the asymmetry is exactly as described. Scouting the fix site:

The multipart path at `src/requests/models.py:245` (`RequestField(name=k, ...)`) passes the key through untouched, while the *values* two loops above are normalized (`str(v)` for non-bytes, `field.decode("utf-8")` for bytes keys in the data loop). The urlencoded path never crashes because `urlencode` stringifies keys on the way out. So `data={1: "a"}` works, and the moment `files` flips the encoder to multipart, the raw int reaches urllib3's `escape` → `.translate` → `AttributeError`.

The minimal, consistent fix is to normalize the name the same way the surrounding code normalizes everything else, at the same one place:

```python
rf = RequestField(
    name=k.decode("utf-8") if isinstance(k, bytes) else str(k),
    data=fdata, filename=fn, headers=fh,
)
```

Notes for review:

- `str(k)` matches the value behavior five lines above (values are already `str()`-coerced) and the urlencoded path's eventual `urlencode` stringification — so `files={1: b"x"}` would send a `1` field name, same as `data={1: "a"}` sends `1=a`. Consistency argues for coercion, not `TypeError`.
- The `isinstance(k, bytes)` branch mirrors the data-field loop's `field.decode("utf-8")` (bytes keys crash at the identical site today, with the same `AttributeError`).
- Same file, same function, one statement — no behavior change for str keys, which is the entire existing test corpus.
- Test sketch: `prepare()` a multipart request with `data={1: "a"}, files={"f": b"x"}` and with `files={1: b"x"}`, assert `prepare().body` contains `name="1"`; assert bytes key `b"field"` yields `name="field"`.

Happy to open a PR for this if nobody's claimed it.

Withdrawing my offer to open a PR: `.github/AI_POLICY.md` explicitly excludes agentic tools from submitting, and a patch authored under agent control can't certify the authorship clause. Leaving the analysis above for whoever picks this up — the one-line normalization at `models.py:245` (str-coerce, decode bytes keys) keeps the name behavior consistent with the value normalization already in the same function.

The issue can be reproduced locally. When a non-string field name is used in a request with file attachments, it raises an `AttributeError`.
Before working on a fix, I would like to clarify the intended behavior. Would it be preferable to convert non-string field names to strings for consistency, or to raise a `TypeError` for invalid field names?

In 2.33.1 both used `compat.cookielib`. If `http.cookiejar` ends up loaded twice.

This is only reproducable under PyCharms Behave runner.
Works with 2.34.0 with plain behave in a terminal.
Works also with 2.33.1 with PyCharms Behave runner.

## Expected Result

No  "ValueError: You can only merge into CookieJar" using Pycharms behave runner with 2.34.0 or later.

title: TestTimeout abandons three delay/10 requests and later tests wait out the server
body:
`TestTimeout` makes three requests to `httpbin("delay/10")` and abandons all of them:

- `tests/test_requests.py:2539`, `test_stream_timeout`, `timeout=2.0`
- `tests/test_requests.py:2573`, `test_read_timeout`, parametrized, `timeout=0.1` (two params)

The client raises at 2.0s and 0.1s, but the pytest-httpbin server keeps sleeping the full 10 seconds and serves requests serially. The next test that needs the server blocks until those sleeps finish.

```
$ pytest "tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_encoded_methods" -p no:randomly
1 passed in 0.56s

$ pytest "tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_read_timeout" \
         "tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_encoded_methods" \
         -p no:randomly --durations=5
19.79s call     tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_encoded_methods
 0.11s call     tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_read_timeout[timeout1]
 0.10s call     tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_read_timeout[timeout0]
3 passed in 20.55s
```

`test_encoded_methods` is one line (`requests.request(b"GET", httpbin("get"))`). The 19.79s is 2 x 10s of server sleep minus the 0.2s the two clients used. In a full run the cost lands on whichever tests happen to follow:

```
19.35s call     TestTimeout::test_encoded_methods
 8.00s call     TestTimeout::test_none_timeout[None]
```

Both call sites need the server to outlast the client timeout, not to sleep for 10 seconds. Lowering the delays leaves the assertions unchanged:

- line 2539, `delay/10` to `delay/3` (client timeout 2.0)
- line 2573, `delay/10` to `delay/1` (client timeout 0.1)

With that change, `TestTimeout` goes from 30.56s to 5.70s and the full suite from 167.44s to 142.04s, with the same results either way: 630 passed, 3 skipped, 1 xpassed. The single failure in both runs is `TestPreparingURLs::test_different_connection_pool_for_tls_settings_verify_bundle_unexpired_cert`, which is unrelated and fails before the change as well.

Measured at 611c616 on Windows 11, Python 3.14.2, pytest 9.1.1.

title: proxy_bypass_registry uses unanchored re.match (Windows proxy bypass)
body:
This was discussed here multiple times in the past so I'm opening it as a public bug report.

`src/requests/utils.py`, `proxy_bypass_registry` (main, 2.34.2):

```python
if re.match(test, host, re.I):   # start-anchored only
    return True
```

re.match anchors only the start, so ProxyOverride=google.com matches google.com.evil.com and bypasses the proxy for it — an attacker-influenced hostname can escape a proxy meant to inspect traffic.

Diverges from CPython: this is a copy of CPython's old code. CPython now matches with fnmatch (anchored both ends, wildcards preserved). Verified on 3.14:
- `fnmatch("google.com.evil.com", "google.com")` → False (requests returns True)
- `fnmatch("a.example.net", "*.example.net")` → True

Fix: use fnmatch(host, test) to match CPython, or minimally anchor: re.match(test + r"\Z", host, re.I).

comments_snapshot.body: Thanks for the issue, @frenzymadness. We're already tracking this work for our next release.

Not blocking — I know this is already tracked for the next release, just leaving a tested reference fix in case it's useful.

One-line change in `proxy_bypass_registry`: anchor the converted pattern so a suffix can't escape it:

```diff
- if re.match(test, host, re.I):
+ if re.match(test + r"\Z", host, re.I):
```

Behaviour I verified locally (Windows registry path monkeypatched, Python 3.13):

| override | host | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `google.com` | `google.com.evil.com` | bypassed ❌ | proxied ✅ |
| `internal` | `internal` | bypassed | bypassed ✅ |
| `*.corp` | `a.corp.evil.com` | bypassed ❌ | proxied ✅ |
| `*.corp` | `a.corp` | bypassed | bypassed ✅ |
| `10.0.0.1` | `10.0.0.1x` | bypassed ❌ | proxied ✅ |

Existing exact and wildcard entries keep working because `fnmatch.translate` already emits `\Z` for them; only the plain-entry branch needs the extra anchor.

Branch: https://github.com/ege-arhan/requests/tree/fix/issue-7629 (`e825f8e7` fix + `eb5f5e45` regression tests added to the `test_should_bypass_proxies_win_registry` parametrize block, 5 cases). Happy to close this if the internal patch differs.

I prepared a focused fix for the unanchored Windows ProxyOverride match. Exact entries still match and wildcard entries remain supported, while suffix hosts such as google.com.evil.com no longer bypass the proxy for google.com. Added exact-host and wildcard regression cases; the Windows registry-path tests pass locally (16 passed).

Branch: https://github.com/Maurenz2530/requests/tree/fix-windows-proxy-bypass-anchor
Compare: https://github.com/psf/requests/compare/main...Maurenz2530:fix-windows-proxy-bypass-anchor
Commit: 6bfa9105

I understand this is already tracked for a future release. GitHub does not allow me to open an upstream PR, so I’m sharing the tested branch in case it is useful to review or pull in.

I have a tested fix for this ready, but GitHub is currently refusing to let this account open a pull request against `psf/requests` (`CreatePullRequest` permission denied), so posting the patch here for a maintainer to apply or to let me open.

- branch: [`januththedev/requests:fix/proxy-override-anchor`](https://github.com/januththedev/requests/tree/fix/proxy-override-anchor)
- commit: `7b68766`

## The change

`src/requests/utils.py`:

```diff
             test = test.replace(".", r"\.")  # mask dots
             test = test.replace("*", r".*")  # change glob sequence
             test = test.replace("?", r".")  # change glob char
-            if re.match(test, host, re.I):
+            # The whole host must match. re.match only anchors the start, so
+            # "example.com" would also bypass the proxy for "example.com.evil.net".
+            if re.fullmatch(test, host, re.I):
                 return True
         return False
```

`re.fullmatch` is the smallest change that makes the intent explicit, and it matches what the `no_proxy` path already does — `test_should_bypass_proxies` in `tests/test_utils.py` already covers "does not greedily match domains that merely endswith the no_proxy entry. See CPython bpo-39057", so the registry path was the one left on the old behaviour.

The `<local>` branch above returns before reaching the pattern match, so it is unaffected.

## Tests

Four cases added to the existing `test_should_bypass_proxies_win_registry` table — two that fail before the change, and two controls that already passed:

| URL | ProxyOverride | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `http://example.com.evil.net/` | `example.com` | `False` (was `True`) |
| `http://notexample.com/` | `example.com` | `False` (control, unchanged) |
| `http://www.example.com/` | `*.example.com` | `True` (control: globs still work) |
| `http://www.example.com.evil.net/` | `*.example.com` | `False` (was `True`) |

- Before: `2 failed, 14 passed`.
- After: `16 passed`.
- `pytest tests/test_utils.py` → 232 passed, 1 skipped.
- `ruff check` clean on both files.

The new cases inherit the existing `skipif(os.name != "nt")` guard, since `proxy_bypass_registry` only exists on `win32`.

### Root cause

`proxy_bypass_registry()` in `src/requests/utils.py` builds a pattern from the Windows `ProxyOverride` registry value and matches it with `re.match()`, which **only anchors the start**. An override for `google.com` therefore also matched `google.com.evil.com`:

```python
test = test.replace(".", r"\.")   # mask dots
test = test.replace("*", r".*")   # change glob sequence
test = test.replace("?", r".")    # change glob char
if re.match(test, host, re.I):    # start-anchored only
    return True
```

Consequence: an attacker-influenced hostname can escape a proxy that was configured to inspect its traffic.

### Fix

Append `\Z` so the override must match the entire host:

```python
if re.match(test + r"\Z", host, re.I):
    return True
```

The glob translation is untouched, so existing overrides (`*.example.net`, `?`, etc.) keep behaving exactly as before — only unanchored suffix matches are now rejected.

Note: this function descends from an old copy of CPython's `proxy_bypass`, which now matches with `fnmatch` (anchored at both ends, wildcards preserved). Anchoring here is the **minimal** fix with no change to glob semantics; switching to `fnmatch` would also resolve the issue and better tracks CPython, if maintainers prefer that direction.

### Verification

Reproduced locally on Windows (Python 3.13, requests main @ `448d64a`-era):

- Before fix: `proxy_bypass_registry("google.com.evil.com")` → `True` (the bypass)
- After fix: `False`, while `google.com` → `True` and `*.example.net` still matches `a.example.net` → `True`
- Full `tests/test_utils.py`: 229 passed, 1 skipped

### Patch and regression test

This repository limits pull request creation to collaborators, so the branch is available on my fork instead:

- Branch: `https://github.com/Xx-173/requests/tree/fix/proxy-bypass-anchored-match`
- Commit: `3984164e`

It contains the one-line fix above plus `test_proxy_bypass_registry_does_not_match_host_suffixes` in `tests/test_utils.py` (Windows-only, matching the existing registry tests), which asserts:

- `proxy_bypass_registry("google.com")` is `True` (exact override still works)
- `proxy_bypass_registry("a.example.net")` is `True` (`*.example.net` glob still works)
- `proxy_bypass_registry("google.com.evil.com")` is `False` (suffix escape blocked)
- `proxy_bypass_registry("notgoogle.com")` is `False`

The test fails without the fix and passes with it.

Happy to turn this into a proper PR if collaborator status is granted, or feel free to cherry-pick from the branch above.

title: Docstring examples in `from_key_val_list` show the pre-3.12 OrderedDict repr
body:
`src/requests/utils.py`'s `from_key_val_list` docstring shows:

    >>> from_key_val_list([('key', 'val')])
    OrderedDict([('key', 'val')])

Since Python 3.12, `collections.OrderedDict.__repr__` uses the regular dict form ([cpython gh-101446](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/101446)), so on any currently supported Python this actually prints:

    OrderedDict({'key': 'val'})

Reproducer (Python 3.13.5, requests 2.34.2):

```
>>> from requests.utils import from_key_val_list
>>> from_key_val_list([('key', 'val')])
OrderedDict({'key': 'val'})
>>> from_key_val_list({'key': 'val'})
OrderedDict({'key': 'val'})
```

The `ValueError` example in the same docstring is still accurate. Both stale occurrences are on lines 351 and 357, and a grep of the rest of the package found no others.

I have a two-line fix ready on a fork and would be glad to open a pull request if that's welcome. (The compare page says PRs are limited to collaborators, hence this issue.)

title: API-provided proxies are silently overridden by environment variables; no per-request opt-out

labels.name: actions/autoclose-feat
labels.description: Used for automation to auto-close an issue

body:
Summary
Requests automatically uses environment proxies from HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, etc. There is currently no clean per-request way to disable this behavior. The only reliable workaround is to create a Session and set ```session.trust_env = False.```

Current behavior
When proxy-related environment variables are present, a simple request such as:
```
requests.get(url, proxies={})
```
still uses the environment proxy. Passing an empty proxies dict does not mean “disable all proxies”; it means “no API-level proxy was provided”, so environment proxies are merged in by Session.merge_environment_settings() when trust_env is True.

To actually bypass environment proxies, users must write:

```
session = requests.Session()
session.trust_env = False
session.get(url)
```
They cannot write:

```
requests.get(url, trust_env=False)
```
Expected behavior
I would like one of the following:
`proxies={}` (or explicit None values) to reliably disable all proxies for that request, including environment proxies; or`trust_env `to be accepted as a per-request argument, e.g. `requests.get(url, trust_env=False)`.

Why this matters
Simple scripts and library wrappers cannot easily switch to a Session.

CI / container environments often set `HTTP_PROXY `/ `HTTPS_PROXY `globally.

Some requests need to use the system proxy while others need to bypass it.

Forcing every caller to create and configure a Session adds unnecessary boilerplate.

Recent proxy-related changes, such as stricter proxy URL parsing in 2.32.0+, make this behavior more visible and harder to work around.

Workaround
Currently the only reliable workaround is:

```
session = requests.Session()
session.trust_env = False
response = session.get(url)
```
This works, but it is not convenient and cannot be applied directly to top-level requests.get() / requests.post() calls.

Proposed API
Allow `trust_env `to be passed per request:

```
requests.get(url, trust_env=False)
```
Alternatively, define `proxies={} `as an explicit opt-out from all environment proxies.

title: OpenSSL 4 removed built-in logic for SKID and AKID
body:
<!-- Summary. -->

The openssl command used to have built-in logic to automaticaly add
subjectKeyIdentifier and authorityKeyIdentifier to created certificates.
This logic vanished in OpenSSL 4.0 and the extensions are missing.
    
Python 3.13+ uses VERIFY_X509_STRICT to verify the certificate. Missing
those attributes is an error.

## Expected Result

A certificated with SKID and AKID.

## Actual Result

No SKID and AKID.

## Reproduction Steps

```
$ openssl version
OpenSSL 4.0.2 25 Aug 2026 (Library: OpenSSL 4.0.2 25 Aug 2026)
for cert in expired mtls valid/server ; do make -C  tests/certs/$cert clean all; done
pytest -v tests/test_requests.py
```
And then somewhere appears
```
 error = SSLError(SSLCertVerificationError(1, '[SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: Missing Authority Key Identifier (_ssl.c:1082)'))
 _pool = <urllib3.connectionpool.HTTPSConnectionPool object at 0x7f0a6d92a2c0>
 _stacktrace = <traceback object at 0x7f0a6dfa7a80>
....
 FAILED tests/test_requests.py::TestPreparingURLs::test_different_connection_pool_for_tls_settings_verify_bundle_unexpired_cert
```

I prepared https://github.com/sebastianas/requests/commit/339333739074118a93a9f496981b394e94bc1690 as a fix but can't open a pull request.

Sebastian

comments_snapshot.body:
I'd like to take this one. Python 3.13+ adopting `VERIFY_X509_STRICT` flips the default to 'reject certs without SKID/AKID' for the stdlib `ssl` module. The `requests` package historically expected OpenSSL to add SKID/AKID automatically; OpenSSL 4 dropped that auto-add. So a cert that worked under Python 3.12 / OpenSSL 1.x now fails VERIFY_X509_STRICT under Python 3.13+ / OpenSSL 4.

**Root cause.** In `requests/adapters.py` (the `send` method's TLS branch) `ssl_wrap_socket` is called without any post-handshake check; the SKID/AKID handling lives entirely in the underlying OpenSSL. With OpenSSL 4, the auto-add logic is removed (`apps/openssl` CLI / `X509V3_EXT_nconf` behavior change), so any cert without explicit SKID/AKID fails Python 3.13+ `VERIFY_X509_STRICT`.

**Alternatives I considered:** (a) Document the breakage: 'if you're on OpenSSL 4 + Python 3.13+, add SKID/AKID to your cert manually or via your CA tool' (workaround). (b) Add a post-handshake check in `requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter` that logs a warning when the cert lacks SKID/AKID and the user has `verify=True` (best UX, IMO). (c) Patch urllib3 to retry / re-issue — too deep, out of scope.

**Suggestion to maintainer:** I'd go (b) — a clear warning log + a doc paragraph. Two questions: (i) Does `requests` want to vendor a tiny helper that, when the server cert lacks SKID/AKID, fetches the issuer cert from the chain and validates? (probably too much). (ii) Is the affected Python version (3.13+) one that `requests` is *required* to support per its compatibility matrix? (claiming via @LeonxLJX)

title: Drop the versionless `License ::` classifier now that `license` is a valid SPDX expression
body:
> This issue is part of a larger batch of similar-scoped issues we distribute in the context of our internal vulnerability and dependency tracking activities. The batch covers multiple projects, this is only one of them. The goal is to rise awareness and trigger/initiate the change towards clean project metadata in projects we depend on.

## Summary

This project already declares a valid SPDX license id/expression in its packaging metadata (`License: Apache-2.0` in the built METADATA), but the deprecated classifier `License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License` is still present. That classifier has no version and [PEP 639](https://peps.python.org/pep-0639/)-aware SBOM tooling like [cyclonedx-bom](https://pypi.org/project/cyclonedx-bom/) can't map it to an SPDX id, so it falls back to emitting the raw classifier text as a free-text license name. This free-text field is just noise and causes downstream tooling to flag this project as non-SPDX-compliant.

## Suggested fix

Remove the redundant `License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License` from `classifiers` in the packaging config. No change to the `license` field is needed.

## How to reproduce

```bash
uv tool install cyclonedx-bom
uv venv .venv-repro
uv pip install --python .venv-repro/bin/python requests
cyclonedx-py environment .venv-repro -o sbom.cdx.json
```

... and then check the `.licenses` property of the component. There should only something like:

```json
// This is how it should look like
...
    "license": {
        "acknowledgement": "declared",
        "id": "<VALID SPDX IDENTIFIER>"
    }
...
```

and _not_:

```json
// This is how it should not look like
...
    "license": {
       "acknowledgement": "declared",
       "name": "<CLASSIFIER TAKEN FROM METADATA"
    }
...
```

I'm happy to provide a PR to resolve this timely after approval!

comments_snapshot.body: Why open spammy issues against 10s (if not more) repositories when the tooling could detect "License is a valid SPDX" license, the other information is less accurate and should be ignored. CycloneDX seems to be actively maintained. Why make individual projects do work that doesn't help on older versions instead of fixing the broken tool?

We evaluated our third part dependencies and decided to make the packages/repositories/maintainers aware of this circumstance. Since lots of the projects used by us share the same problem, using a template-like issue which is specific enough and actionable seemed to be justified. 

The license classifier used by requests is deprecated (see https://peps.python.org/pep-0639/#deprecate-license-classifiers), so the fix needs to be done here anyways. 

The cyclonedx-bom tool does what it should, since the CycloneDX 1.7 specification allows free-text fields (https://cyclonedx.org/docs/1.7/json/#metadata_tools_oneOf_i0_components_items_licenses_items_oneOf_i0_license_name). The problem is that the requests package has a single license defined here https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/5460f467b02e49471c0fd6cfc9ca0adab6351f98/pyproject.toml#L9, but reports multiple in its metadata.

So having the license classifier is not only deprecated but also redundant. Maybe the SBOM example wasn't the best case to justify a need for adjustment, sorry for that. But treating this issue as if it was spam is not adequate.

@btschwertfeger, we have discussed this [here](https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/7012#discussion_r2748329758) previously. The current setup is intended as there are still millions of daily downloads of setuptools that do not support what you're proposing.

We will get to a point where we are able to remove this in the future but forcing projects to follow a deprecation that's happened in the last 6 months is fairly aggressive for the Python ecosystem. We'll revisit in the future, but it's still not clear why Cyclonedx is not able to disambiguate two fairly concrete specifiers. The SPDX identifier we include is synonymous with the classifier. Breaking users ability to build the package for the sake of simplifying metadata tooling is not something we intend to do immediately.
That is fine, at least we now have an issue to track and refer to. 👍

> But treating this issue as if it was spam is not adequate.

I would have closed it if I said it was spam. I said it's spammy because instead of fixing this in one place, you're requiring 10s if not 100s of maintainers to fix this individually and only on the latest version of the package which there's 0 guarantee you'll upgrade to. So your SBOM tool will still misreport things. Instead of fixing CycloneDX you're making work for others with no guarantee of the payoff for you

> > But treating this issue as if it was spam is not adequate.
> 
> I would have closed it if I said it was spam. I said it's spammy because instead of fixing this in one place, you're requiring 10s if not 100s of maintainers to fix this individually and only on the latest version of the package which there's 0 guarantee you'll upgrade to. So your SBOM tool will still misreport things. Instead of fixing CycloneDX you're making work for others with no guarantee of the payoff for you


As I already noted in https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/7610#issuecomment-5425896809 that the cyclonedx-bom example wasn't the best one to make this point. I should have used this: 

```bash
pip3 -q download requests --no-deps
unzip -qo requests-2.34.2-py3-none-any.whl
grep License requests-2.34.2.dist-info/METADATA
License: Apache-2.0
Classifier: License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License
License-File: LICENSE
License-File: NOTICE
```

... proving two declarations of the same license where one of them is deprecated and versionless. So the problem exists in the package metadata itself, independent of any tooling.

I'd argue that "no guarantee of the payoff for you" doesn't apply here. We already have suppressions in place, so nothing here is blocking us or waiting on this fix. This was never about our own pipeline. As for all issues, the maintainers decide if and how to schedule changes. The intent was to create awareness and not to apply pressure or force any kind of urgency. 

"Spammy" doesn't fit either, IMO. Most of the maintainers we contacted across these issues merged a PR or fixed it themselves without much discussion. This one has taken more back and forth than most, but that doesn't make the underlying issue less valid.

This gets cleaned up eventually, just not now, and that's fine for us.

Opened a fix branch for this: https://github.com/psf/requests/compare/main...ShamikOfficial:fix/drop-license-classifier?quick_pull=1

Single-line removal of the obsolete `License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License` classifier in `pyproject.toml`. The SPDX `license = Apache-2.0` field is unchanged.

I've got a one-line fix ready on ShamikOfficial:fix/drop-license-classifier (drops the obsolete License classifier; keeps Apache-2.0). Attempting to open the PR now; if GitHub blocks PR creation for non-collaborators on this repo, please shout and I can adjust.

title: Should Authorization header be cleared in https -> http redirect?

comments_snapshot.body: From what I can tell by experiment, Firefox and Chromium treat http and https versions of a site as separate authentication realms, and don't automatically reuse basic credentials on either a redirect or manual browsing between the two. Two http URLs with the same host (localhost) and different port numbers also seem to be treated as independent realms.

Found something about it in [RFC 7235, section 2.2](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7235#section-2.2).
> A protection space is defined by the canonical root URI (the scheme and authority components of the effective request URI; see Section 5.5 of [RFC7230]) of the server being accessed, in combination with the realm value if present.

which suggests that both the scheme and port number should be considered (and in theory one should also check the realm, but that doesn't really fit into request's model that basic credentials are supplied unconditionally rather than in response to WWW-Authentication).
is this going to get a release?
Yes @thinkt4nk, we’re currently coordinating a release with the urllib3 team.
